steps.label: Deeper but worse is not always overfitting · 1/3

narration.label: p0-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The left panel defines degradation: after adding depth, even training accuracy saturates or declines. Ask whether optimization is actually using the deeper model’s available capacity. A model may be able to represent a good function without the training procedure finding its parameters. These panels describe the problems conceptually; they are not invented empirical curves or numerical results from an experiment.

steps.speakerNotes: Deeper but worse is not always overfitting · 1/3 · Female: The left panel defines degradation: after adding depth, even training accuracy saturates or declines. Ask whether optimization is actually using the deeper model’s available capacity. A model may be able to represent a good function without the training procedure finding its parameters. These panels describe the problems conceptually; they are not invented empirical curves or numerical results from an experiment.

steps.label: Deeper but worse is not always overfitting · 2/3

narration.label: p0-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The right panel defines a typical overfitting pattern: good training performance but poor test performance. Its central issue is a generalization gap, unlike the degradation panel where training itself becomes worse. The lecture’s observation near twenty layers is not a universal hard threshold. Diagnose what happens on training and test data separately before naming the problem or choosing a remedy.

steps.speakerNotes: Deeper but worse is not always overfitting · 2/3 · Female: The right panel defines a typical overfitting pattern: good training performance but poor test performance. Its central issue is a generalization gap, unlike the degradation panel where training itself becomes worse. The lecture’s observation near twenty layers is not a universal hard threshold. Diagnose what happens on training and test data separately before naming the problem or choosing a remedy.

steps.label: Deeper but worse is not always overfitting · 3/3

narration.label: p0-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The conclusion separates representational capacity from optimization success. If a deeper network has worse training accuracy as well as worse test accuracy, is overfitting automatically the right explanation? No. The training result motivates investigating degradation and optimization. A network’s ability to express a solution does not establish that its training process reached that solution.

steps.label: Learn a correction; add the input through a shortcut · 1/3

narration.label: p1-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The main path and shortcut parameterize a desired transformation H as F plus the input x. Define F as H minus x: it learns the correction that remains after the shortcut supplies the input unchanged. The two paths merge by elementwise addition, not by widening channels through concatenation. The main path still learns; residual learning does not remove it from optimization.

steps.label: Learn a correction; add the input through a shortcut · 2/3

narration.label: p1-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The numerical example below makes the addition concrete. Input one and main-path output 0.5 give total output 1.5. If the main path instead outputs zero, the block output equals its input. This gives a simple way to express no change, while allowing nonzero corrections when useful. The diagram shows a block-level relationship and deliberately leaves other activation and normalization details unexpanded.

steps.label: Learn a correction; add the input through a shortcut · 3/3

narration.label: p1-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway is that identity requires zero correction, not shutting down learning forever. If the shortcut passes input one and the main path outputs minus 0.2, what does the addition produce? It produces 0.8. The shortcut supplies a reference value, and the learned residual can increase or decrease it depending on the task.

steps.label: Residual parameterization makes identity easy to express · 1/3

narration.label: p2-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Compare the two representations of identity. In an ordinary stack, the entire composed transformation must equal the input. With residual parameterization, the shortcut already provides that input, so the main path only needs to output zero. Both can represent identity. The distinction is how the parameterization expresses this useful special case, rather than a claim that ordinary layers are mathematically incapable of it.

steps.label: Residual parameterization makes identity easy to express · 2/3

narration.label: p2-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The lower relation states that zero F implies H equals x. No extra correction remains after adding the shortcut. This describes an available representational setting, not a guarantee that every optimization run converges to it. When changing the input is useful, the main path can instead learn a nonzero residual. Residual learning is therefore not restricted to copying data.

steps.label: Residual parameterization makes identity easy to express · 3/3

narration.label: p2-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The bottom statement limits the argument to expressibility. Does making identity easy to write prove that every deeper network will train better on every dataset? No. Optimization, initialization, normalization, and the task still matter. The structural argument explains a helpful starting point for residual learning without converting it into a universal performance theorem.

steps.label: Align shapes before adding the shortcut · 1/3

narration.label: p3-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The input has sixty-four channels, but the main path outputs one hundred twenty-eight. An unchanged shortcut therefore has the wrong shape for direct addition. The displayed one-by-one projection transforms the shortcut to one hundred twenty-eight channels as well. Height and width are fixed in this example. This aligns two inputs for addition; it is not a concatenation of unequal-width feature collections.

steps.label: Align shapes before adding the shortcut · 2/3

narration.label: p3-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The addition and lower reminder require both paths to match in height, width, and channel count. If the main path also reduces spatial dimensions, shortcut stride must follow that change. A projection convolution has learned weights and additional computation. It cannot be described as a zero-parameter identity shortcut merely because it occupies the shortcut branch of a residual block.

steps.label: Align shapes before adding the shortcut · 3/3

narration.label: p3-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway distinguishes identity from projection. Can a sixty-four-channel identity shortcut be added directly to a one-hundred-twenty-eight-channel main output? Not without alignment. Here the projection supplies that alignment. Whenever reporting shortcut parameter cost, specify whether the shortcut copies its input unchanged or applies a learned transformation.

steps.label: The shortcut contributes an extra one to the derivative · 1/3

narration.label: p4-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The single-block derivative follows directly from H equals F plus x. Differentiating with respect to x gives the derivative of F plus one. That one comes from the identity shortcut; it is not an artificial instruction setting every gradient to one. If the residual derivative is small, the block derivative may be near one, which helps explain the more direct route for propagating changes.

steps.label: The shortcut contributes an extra one to the derivative · 2/3

narration.label: p4-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The three blocks and lower product apply the chain rule. Multiply each block’s one-plus-residual-derivative factor to obtain the overall derivative. The result still depends on every factor and does not automatically equal one. This is a scalar derivation; the vector version uses Jacobian matrices plus identity matrices. A scalar multiplication example is not a guarantee of identical behavior in every vector direction.

steps.label: The shortcut contributes an extra one to the derivative · 3/3

narration.label: p4-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The conclusion is conditional. If the residual derivative is approximately zero, what is the scalar block derivative? Approximately one. If the residual derivative is large, negative, or varies strongly across blocks, that simple favorable picture can fail. The shortcut changes the derivative structure but does not remove the need to analyze the actual factors.

narration.label: p5-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Read the horizontal axis as layer or block count and the logarithmic vertical axis as the magnitude of a derivative product. These are hypothetical scalar factors, not measured network gradients. Compare curves at the same depth. A factor that looks only moderately different from one can create a large change after repeated multiplication, so the first layer alone does not reveal the full effect.

narration.label: p5-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway is proximity to one, under the displayed conditions. Does using a residual architecture force every actual block derivative to be 0.95 or 1.05? No. Those are selected demonstration values. Their products show why near-one factors can avoid rapid decay, while also reminding us that slightly larger factors can accumulate growth.

narration.label: p6-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The left card counts the same two-layer main path in both comparisons. Each convolution is three-by-three with sixty-four input and output channels. Two times nine times sixty-four squared gives seventy-three thousand seven hundred twenty-eight weights. Biases, projection, and normalization parameters are excluded. Holding that main path fixed isolates the extra contribution, if any, of an identity shortcut.

steps.label: An identity shortcut adds no weights, but still adds computation · 2/3

narration.label: p6-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The right card passes x directly to the addition, requiring zero learned weights. However, combining the two paths still performs an elementwise addition, so zero parameters does not mean zero computation. A projection shortcut is a different case: its convolution adds both learned weights and arithmetic. Always identify the shortcut type before applying the zero-parameter statement.

steps.label: An identity shortcut adds no weights, but still adds computation · 3/3

narration.label: p6-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The conclusion separates parameter storage from operations. If the unchanged main path receives an identity shortcut, do its convolution weights suddenly double? No. The shortcut adds no learned weights in this comparison, but it adds an addition operation. That limited claim should not be extended to projection shortcuts or interpreted as saying the entire residual block is free.

steps.label: Residual learning helps, but does not guarantee stable scale · 1/3

narration.label: p7-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The three visible blocks each multiply their input by 1.1. The main path keeps adding a residual equal to one tenth of that block’s input, in the same direction as the shortcut value. A small repeated increase can accumulate. Only three blocks are drawn; the lower ten-block calculation continues exactly the same rule rather than introducing seven unseen operations of a different kind.

steps.label: Residual learning helps, but does not guarantee stable scale · 2/3

narration.label: p7-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The formula gives F of x as 0.1 times x, so each whole block returns 1.1 times x. Ten blocks multiply the input by 1.1 to the tenth power, about 2.594. This counterexample shows that the shortcut does not automatically preserve activation scale. Suitable initialization and normalization still matter, and actual training values should be monitored rather than assumed stable from the architecture name.

steps.label: Residual learning helps, but does not guarantee stable scale · 3/3

narration.label: p7-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway limits what residual learning guarantees. If every block adds an aligned positive correction, can the output grow even though shortcuts exist? Yes, as the ten-block factor demonstrates. An extra route can ease optimization without substituting for the other conditions needed to control signal size and gradients.

A one-by-one convolution reduces channels; a three-by-three convolution performs spatial processing at that narrower width; another one-by-one convolution restores channels. Deeper fifty- and one-hundred-one-layer versions commonly use this pattern. The diagram shows the main path only; the residual shortcut and addition still follow the earlier block idea. These three kernels are not a picture of the entire network.
